API Reference EHR Integration REST API
Healthcare · HIPAA-adjacent

An API reference manual for third-party integrations with a clinical EHR backend. Documents authentication flows, endpoint contracts, payload schemas, and error-handling states for engineering teams building on top of patient data infrastructure.

ehr-api-reference.md

Authentication

All requests must include a valid Bearer token in the Authorization header. Tokens are issued through the /v2/auth/token endpoint and expire after 3,600 seconds. Self-signed certificates are rejected at the API Gateway; only tokens signed by the platform's certificate authority are accepted.

Token verification happens at the gateway, one hop before the request reaches any endpoint that touches patient data. This ordering is intentional: an invalid token never gets close enough to a patient record to matter, which is also why the 401 response carries no detail about which record was being requested. A client that retries on 401 should always re-authenticate first. Retrying the original request with the same expired token wastes a round trip and produces an identical rejection, since the gateway does not grant any grace window after expiry.

Refresh tokens are not issued. When a bearer token expires mid-session, the client calls /v2/auth/token again with its original client credentials. This keeps the auth surface to one code path instead of two, at the cost of one extra round trip every hour for long-lived integrations; teams running high-frequency sync jobs should account for that in their retry budget rather than treating a 401 as an unexpected failure.

Endpoint Reference

Method Endpoint Access Description
POST /v2/ehr/patients/sync Write / Read Initiates a streaming sync pipeline for clinical data updates. Accepts a patient UUID and returns a sync session token.
GET /v2/ehr/patients/query Read only Retrieves patient records by cryptographic UUID. Returns paginated results. Supports ?fields= projection for bandwidth-sensitive clients.
PATCH /v2/ehr/patients/:uuid/vitals Write Updates a patient's vital sign record. Partial updates are supported; omitted fields are not modified.
DELETE /v2/ehr/patients/:uuid/session Write Terminates an active sync session and revokes its session token. Idempotent: returns 200 even if the session has already expired.

Error States

  • 401 Unauthorized — Token is missing, malformed, or expired. Re-authenticate via /v2/auth/token.
  • 403 Forbidden — Token is valid but the caller's access tier does not permit this operation.
  • 422 Unprocessable Entity — Payload failed schema validation. The response body includes a validation_errors array with field-level details.
  • 429 Too Many Requests — Rate limit exceeded. Retry after the duration in the Retry-After header.

Rate Limiting and Idempotency

Each access tier carries a distinct rate budget: 120 requests per minute for read-only clients, 40 requests per minute for clients with write access. The budget is enforced per token, not per IP, so rotating tokens does not raise the effective limit. A 429 response always includes Retry-After in seconds; clients that back off by this value rather than a fixed interval see meaningfully fewer repeated rejections in practice, since the header reflects the actual remaining window rather than a worst-case estimate.

Write endpoints that mutate state — PATCH and DELETE — accept an optional Idempotency-Key header. When present, a repeated request with the same key and the same payload within a 24-hour window returns the original response rather than re-applying the mutation. This matters most for PATCH /vitals: a client that times out waiting for a response and retries without an idempotency key risks writing the same vital-sign update twice, which in a clinical record is not a harmless duplicate but a timestamp discrepancy someone eventually has to reconcile by hand.

ehr_payload_schema.json 
// POST /v2/ehr/patients/sync — Request Body
{
  "request_id": "req_01HJ8Z4K",
  "patient_uuid": "8b9a4bc2-91ef-4d3c-b210-c0e2a1f39b7d",
  "sync_mode": "incremental",       // "full" | "incremental"
  "clinical_payload": {
    "systolic_bp": 120,
    "diastolic_bp": 80,
    "heart_rate": 72,
    "spo2": 98.4,
    "recorded_at": "2026-10-17T12:00:00Z",
    "status": "STABLE"
  }
}

// 200 OK — Response
{
  "sync_session": "sess_xM9jQpR7",
  "status": "ACCEPTED",
  "ttl_seconds": 300,
  "next_poll_url": "/v2/ehr/sync/sess_xM9jQpR7/status"
}
Technical Spec ML Computer Vision Inference Pipeline
AI / Medical Imaging · DICOM

A reference architecture document for a DICOM-to-inference pipeline. Written for ML engineers integrating a computer vision model into a radiology workflow. Covers ingestion, preprocessing, model execution, and output interpretation, including the failure paths at each stage.

cv-inference-pipeline-spec.md

Architecture Overview

The pipeline accepts raw DICOM files, normalizes them to a 512×512 float32 array, and passes the result to the inference engine. All steps run sequentially in the same process; no async queuing is introduced before anomaly detection completes, to preserve audit-log linearity. This is a deliberate constraint, not an oversight: a queued pipeline would let a malformed file's quarantine event arrive out of order relative to the audit entries around it, which breaks the assumption every downstream compliance report depends on.

Ingestion and Preprocessing

Each incoming file passes a header integrity check before any pixel data is decoded. Files that fail the check are quarantined and logged with a DICOM_PARSE_ERROR event; they do not enter the preprocessing queue. A quarantined file is retained for 30 days and is retrievable by its original transfer UID through the /v2/quarantine endpoint, so a radiology tech who re-sends a corrected file is not re-uploading from scratch.

  • Window leveling applied at ingestion time using the DICOM WindowCenter and WindowWidth tags when present, or the dataset's p5/p95 intensities as fallback.
  • All frames are resampled to 512×512 using bilinear interpolation.
  • Pixel values are normalized to [0.0, 1.0] before the model receives the tensor.
  • Multi-frame studies are split into individual frames before inference; the response payload re-associates each detection with its source frame index.

Model Execution

The inference step targets layer weights at index 14 of the production ResNet-50 backbone (exported as ONNX, quantized INT8). The model returns bounding box coordinates and a per-box confidence score for each detected anomaly region. Quantization was chosen over the full-precision model after benchmarking showed a 3.6x latency improvement with less than a 0.4-point drop in recall on the validation set; that trade-off is the reason INT8 appears in the model version string rather than being left implicit.

Output Interpretation

A confidence threshold of 0.92 is the production default. Boxes below this threshold are excluded from the response payload but retained in the raw inference log for audit purposes, which matters for any later review of a missed detection: the evidence that the model saw something is preserved even when it did not clear the bar to surface. Output coordinates use the DICOM image coordinate space, not the normalized 512×512 space, so a downstream viewer can draw the box directly on the original image without an extra transform.

inference_response.json 
// POST /v2/inference/run — Response (200 OK)
{
  "request_id": "inf_03GH1A9F",
  "image_uid": "1.2.840.10008.5.1.4.1.1.2",
  "processing_ms": 187,
  "model_version": "resnet50-int8-v2.3.1",
  "detections": [
    {
      "detection_id": "det_001",
      "layer_index": 14,
      "confidence": 0.984,
      "anomaly_detected": false,
      "bounding_box": {
        "x1": 112, "y1": 88,
        "x2": 340, "y2": 290
      },
      "coordinate_space": "DICOM_IMAGE"
    }
  ],
  "audit_log_id": "alog_7X2mNq"
}
Developer Guide LLM Prompt Engineering Guide
AI Systems · Developer Onboarding

A conceptual guide written for software engineers integrating an LLM API for the first time. Translates model behavior into engineering-friendly mental models, covering token budgets, context windows, temperature, and output determinism.

llm-integration-guide.md

Conceptual Guide

The context window is not infinite memory

Every request to an LLM API is stateless. The model has no memory of previous requests. What it knows is only what you put in the messages array of the current call. The "context window" is the maximum number of tokens the model can read in a single request, including both your input and the space it needs to generate a response.

A practical rule: if your application needs the model to remember something across turns, you are responsible for including it in the next request. Session memory is an engineering problem, not a model feature.

Temperature controls how surprising the output is

Setting temperature: 0 makes the model nearly deterministic — it will almost always produce the same output for the same input. Setting it higher (towards 1.0 or above) introduces more variation. For documentation generation, structured data extraction, or any task where consistency matters, keep temperature at or near 0. For creative generation, raise it.

Token limits apply to input and output separately

The max_tokens parameter caps the output length only. A long system prompt plus a long user message can exceed the context window before the model writes a single token in return. Count your input tokens before you send, especially in loops where conversation history accumulates. A conversation that silently fails on turn 40 because history outgrew the window is one of the more common support tickets in LLM integrations, and it is avoidable entirely by tracking token count as a running total rather than discovering the ceiling by hitting it.

In practice this means treating token budget as a resource to manage, the same way you would manage memory in a long-running process. Two strategies cover most cases. The first is a sliding window: once history approaches a set threshold, drop the oldest turns rather than the newest, since recent context is almost always more relevant to the current request. The second is summarization: periodically replace a block of old turns with a short generated summary of what was discussed, trading some fidelity for a bounded token cost. Neither is free; both require the application, not the model, to decide what gets kept.

Streaming changes what "done" means

A streamed response arrives as a sequence of partial chunks rather than one complete payload. This is the right default for anything rendered to a user in real time, since perceived latency drops even though total generation time does not change. It also changes the integration contract: your code needs to handle a connection that closes mid-stream, reassemble chunks in order, and detect the model's own stop signal separately from a network-level disconnect. Treating a dropped connection and a clean stop as the same event is a common source of truncated output that looks correct until a user notices a sentence ending mid-word.

For structured output — JSON a downstream system will parse — streaming adds a real cost: a partial JSON object is not valid JSON, so code that tries to parse each chunk as it arrives will fail until the final chunk completes the structure. The practical rule is to stream only what a human will read directly, and to request a single complete response for anything a machine will parse next.

Retries need a backoff strategy, not a loop

Rate limit and server-error responses are expected traffic at any meaningful request volume, not exceptions. A naive retry loop that immediately resends on failure tends to make rate limiting worse, since every client backing off at the same instant creates a new burst the moment the window resets. Exponential backoff with jitter — waiting a randomized, increasing interval between attempts — spreads retries out and is the difference between a transient error recovering invisibly and a cascading failure during a traffic spike.

System Doc AI Agent Behavior Specification
AI / Internal Documentation

An internal technical specification describing how an AI agent decides when to use a tool, how it handles ambiguous inputs, and when it escalates to a human reviewer. Written for engineering teams onboarding to an AI-assisted workflow, where the cost of an undocumented edge case is a silent wrong answer in production.

agent-behavior-spec.md

Behavior Specification

Tool selection logic

The agent evaluates three conditions before selecting a tool: whether the task requires external data, whether the user's intent is unambiguous, and whether the tool's output format matches what the current task expects. If any of these three conditions is uncertain, the agent asks for clarification before calling the tool. It does not attempt tool calls on partial information, because a tool call made on a guessed parameter is harder to detect as wrong than an unanswered question, and it is the detectability of the failure that this rule is protecting.

Ambiguity handling

When the agent cannot determine the user's intent with high confidence, it surfaces its two most probable interpretations and asks the user to select one. It does not silently choose the most probable interpretation and proceed, because errors in automated workflows often compound across steps: a wrong assumption made at step one is invisible until step four produces output that looks plausible but rests on it. A clarified request re-enters the same confidence check rather than being treated as automatically resolved, since a user's one-word answer to a clarifying question can itself be ambiguous.

Human escalation triggers

The agent escalates to a human reviewer whenever: a tool call fails twice consecutively, the user's instruction contradicts a constraint in the system prompt, or the confidence score on a classification output falls below 0.75. All escalations write a structured event to the audit log before handing off, including the agent's last three reasoning steps, so the reviewer inherits context instead of starting cold. The two-failure threshold on tool calls, rather than one, exists because a single transient network error is common and not informative; two consecutive failures against the same tool is the signal worth a human's attention.

State carried across steps

The agent does not re-derive context on every step. A working memory object, scoped to the current task, carries forward the user's original request, any clarification already resolved, and the result of each prior tool call. This is what allows the agent to reference "the file from step two" without re-reading it, but it also means a stale or incorrect value written early can propagate silently through later steps if nothing checks it again. The spec addresses this by requiring that any tool call consuming a value from working memory logs that value alongside its own output, so a reviewer auditing step five can see exactly what step two actually produced, not what step five assumed it produced.

Why this differs from a single-shot classifier

A simpler design would run one classification pass, pick a tool, and execute. That design is easier to reason about and fails more often in exactly the cases that matter: when the input is ambiguous, when the available tools don't cleanly match the request, or when an earlier step's output doesn't satisfy what a later step needs. The decision tree in this spec trades a faster happy path for a system that surfaces its own uncertainty instead of resolving it by guessing. Engineering teams evaluating whether to adopt this pattern should weigh that trade-off directly: it costs additional latency and, for ambiguous requests, an extra round trip to the user. The alternative cost is a wrong tool call that looks like a successful one until someone downstream notices the output doesn't make sense.

Testing the escalation boundary

Three test categories cover this spec in practice. Golden-path tests confirm that clear, well-formed requests reach a tool call without triggering clarification. Ambiguity tests feed intentionally underspecified requests and assert that the agent asks rather than guesses. Escalation tests simulate each of the three triggers individually — repeated tool failure, a contradicted constraint, and sub-threshold confidence — and assert both that escalation fires and that the audit log entry contains the required reasoning trace. A spec without a corresponding test for each named trigger is a description of intended behavior, not a verified one, and the gap between the two is where most production incidents in agentic systems actually originate.

04

How I Work

01
Read the source, not the summary

Before writing a word, I read the codebase, the PR history, or the research paper. I do not document what someone tells me the system does. I document what the system actually does.

02
Write for the reader's failure mode

Every developer guide I write starts from a list of ways the integration could break. Good documentation prevents those failures before they happen — not after a support ticket is raised.

03
Keep structure and prose separate

Tables, code blocks, and schemas carry structure. Paragraphs carry meaning. I do not mix them. When structure replaces prose, the reader gets the skeleton without the reasoning.

04
Treat every edit as a test

Before marking documentation final, I walk through it as a developer seeing it for the first time. If a step could be skipped or misread, it is not finished. Clarity is verified, not assumed.

05

Get in Touch

I am open to freelance technical writing contracts, full-time remote roles, and documentation audits. Response time is usually within 24 hours.
